title: Voltage Divider Under Load
description: A 24 V source feeds R1 (1 kΩ) in series with R2 (2 kΩ). Unloaded, the divider would put 16 V across R2. A 2 kΩ load (RL) is connected across R2. Find what the output voltage actually becomes and why.

tasks.question: What is the total resistance of the loaded divider?
What current does the source supply?
What is the voltage across R1?
What is the loaded output voltage, measured across R2 (and the load)?
What current flows through the load RL?
What power does the load RL dissipate?

hints: Unloaded, the divider rule gives V_R2 = 24 × (2000 ÷ 3000) = 16 V. The load changes that.
RL is in parallel with R2: 2 kΩ ∥ 2 kΩ = 1 kΩ. Now the circuit is 1 kΩ in series with 1 kΩ, a 50/50 split.
Half of 24 V is the loaded output. The drop across R1 rose from 8 V (unloaded) to 12 V because the source current rose from 8 mA to 12 mA.

A divider only holds its voltage if the load resistance is much larger than R2 (ten times or more is a common rule of thumb). This is the same loading effect that makes conductor voltage drop worse as loads are added.
learningGoals: Apply the voltage divider rule and see its limits.
Quantify the loading effect when a load is placed across a divider output.
Connect the loaded divider to real-world voltage drop on conductors.
disclaimer: Simulated bench exercise; not field experience.
